purpose: Deep educational mental models for beginner CLF-C02 learners; not exam dumps or trivia.

entries.name: AWS Regions
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A Region is a separate city/metro area where AWS operates cloud facilities.
entries.plain_english_explanation: A Region is a physical geographic area such as us-east-1 or eu-west-1. You choose a Region to keep workloads near users, meet data residency needs, or isolate disaster-recovery copies. Most resources are regional unless a service is explicitly global.
entries.real_world_use_case: Host EU customer data in an EU Region to reduce latency and support residency expectations.
common_misconceptions: A Region is not one building; it contains multiple AZs. Not all services exist in every Region.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Region is broad location; AZ is isolated location inside it; edge location is for edge delivery/routing.

entries.name: Availability Zones (AZs)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: AZs are separate buildings/neighborhoods inside one city, connected by fast private roads.
entries.plain_english_explanation: An Availability Zone is one or more physically separate data centers inside a Region, with independent power/networking and low-latency links to other AZs. Multi-AZ designs survive data-center-level failures.
entries.real_world_use_case: Run app servers across two AZs behind a load balancer.
common_misconceptions: Two servers in one AZ are not multi-AZ. AZ names can map differently between accounts.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: AZ gives resilience inside a Region; multi-Region is broader DR and more complex.

entries.name: Edge locations
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Edge locations are neighborhood pickup lockers close to users.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Edge locations are AWS global edge sites used by CloudFront, Route 53, and related services to serve cached content or route traffic close to users.
entries.real_world_use_case: Cache static assets close to global website visitors.
common_misconceptions: Edge locations are not Regions and usually do not host full application stacks.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Regions/AZs host workloads; edge locations cache/route traffic.

entries.name: AWS Local Zones
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A Local Zone is a small AWS extension inside a metro area.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Local Zones place select compute, storage, and networking capabilities near large population centers when single-digit millisecond latency to that metro matters.
entries.real_world_use_case: Low-latency gaming, media rendering, or interactive applications in a specific city.
common_misconceptions: Local Zones do not offer every AWS service and are not a replacement for normal Regions.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Local Zones are metro edge; Outposts is in your facility; Wavelength is carrier 5G edge.

entries.name: AWS Wavelength
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Wavelength is a small cloud workbench inside a mobile carrier network.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Wavelength embeds AWS compute/storage at 5G carrier edges for ultra-low-latency mobile applications that should avoid a round trip to a Region.
entries.real_world_use_case: AR/VR, connected vehicles, and live mobile video analytics.
common_misconceptions: Most web apps use Regions plus CloudFront instead of Wavelength.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Wavelength is carrier edge; Local Zones are metro edge; CloudFront is CDN edge.

entries.name: IAM users
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: An IAM user is a named employee badge inside one AWS account.
entries.plain_english_explanation: IAM users are long-term identities in an AWS account. They can sign in or use access keys, but least privilege and MFA are essential, and roles/federation are preferred for many modern patterns.
entries.real_world_use_case: Create a break-glass admin user protected by MFA and rarely used.
common_misconceptions: Do not use the root user for daily work. Access keys are secrets.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Users are identities; groups organize users; roles are assumed temporarily; policies define permissions.

entries.name: IAM groups
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A group is a permissions mailing list for users.
entries.plain_english_explanation: IAM groups collect IAM users so permissions can be attached once for a team instead of repeatedly to individuals.
entries.real_world_use_case: Give a ReadOnly group view-only access for auditors.
common_misconceptions: Groups cannot contain roles or nested groups and are not identities applications assume.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Groups organize users; roles are temporary identities; policies are permission documents.

entries.name: IAM roles
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A role is a temporary costume used to do a job.
entries.plain_english_explanation: IAM roles provide temporary credentials to AWS services, applications, federated users, or other accounts. They avoid hardcoded long-term keys.
entries.real_world_use_case: Give an EC2 instance a role that can read one S3 bucket.
common_misconceptions: A role is not permanently assigned to one person; it is assumed when needed.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Role = temporary assumed permissions; user = long-term identity; policy = permission rules.

entries.name: IAM policies
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A policy is a rule sheet saying who can do which actions on which resources.
entries.plain_english_explanation: IAM policies are JSON permission documents with allow/deny statements, resources, actions, and optional conditions. Least privilege means granting only what is needed.
entries.real_world_use_case: Allow a Lambda function to write to one DynamoDB table and nothing else.
common_misconceptions: Explicit deny overrides allows. A policy alone is not a login identity.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Policies define permissions; IAM identities receive policies; SCPs set org-level maximums.

entries.name: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: MFA is a second lock after the password key.
entries.plain_english_explanation: MFA requires an additional proof such as an authenticator app or hardware key. Cloud Practitioner emphasis: protect root and privileged identities.
entries.real_world_use_case: Enable MFA for root and administrators.
common_misconceptions: MFA does not replace least privilege; it only strengthens authentication.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: MFA verifies login; IAM policies control authorization after login.

entries.name: AWS Key Management Service (KMS)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: KMS is a secure key cabinet used by AWS services.
entries.plain_english_explanation: KMS creates and controls cryptographic keys for encrypting data. Many AWS services integrate with it for managed encryption and auditable key use.
entries.real_world_use_case: Encrypt EBS volumes, S3 objects, and RDS databases with customer managed keys.
common_misconceptions: KMS stores/manages keys, not application passwords or API tokens.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: KMS manages keys; Secrets Manager stores secret values; ACM manages TLS certificates.

entries.name: AWS Secrets Manager
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Secrets Manager is a password vault with optional rotation.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Secrets Manager stores, retrieves, and can rotate secrets such as database passwords and API keys so applications do not hardcode them.
entries.real_world_use_case: Store and rotate an RDS application password.
common_misconceptions: It is not the same as KMS; it stores secret values and uses encryption underneath.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Secrets Manager stores secrets; Parameter Store handles config/simple secrets; KMS handles keys.

entries.name: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: ACM is a certificate office for website ID cards.
entries.plain_english_explanation: ACM provisions, manages, and renews TLS/SSL certificates for AWS-integrated services such as ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway.
entries.real_world_use_case: Add HTTPS to an Application Load Balancer without manual renewal.
common_misconceptions: ACM does not replace DNS or CDN services; it supplies certificates they use.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: ACM manages certificates; KMS manages encryption keys; IAM controls access.

entries.name: AWS Shield
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Shield is a DDoS guard at the edge.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Shield protects against distributed denial-of-service attacks. Shield Standard is automatic; Shield Advanced adds stronger protections and response support.
entries.real_world_use_case: Protect a public web app on CloudFront or Route 53 from DDoS.
common_misconceptions: Shield is not a web request filter for SQL injection; use WAF for that.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Shield handles DDoS; WAF filters web requests; GuardDuty detects suspicious activity.

entries.name: AWS WAF
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: WAF is a bouncer checking HTTP requests before the app.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS WAF controls HTTP/S requests to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and other integrations using rules and managed rule groups.
entries.real_world_use_case: Block known malicious request patterns before they reach a website.
common_misconceptions: WAF is not for every network protocol; it works at web layer.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: WAF filters web requests; Shield absorbs DDoS; security groups control resource traffic.

entries.name: Amazon GuardDuty
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: GuardDuty is a security camera watching logs for suspicious behavior.
entries.plain_english_explanation: GuardDuty analyzes signals such as CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and other sources to detect threats and produce findings.
entries.real_world_use_case: Detect unusual API calls or compromised credential behavior.
common_misconceptions: GuardDuty detects; it does not patch vulnerabilities or become a full SIEM alone.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: GuardDuty detects threats; Inspector finds vulnerabilities; Security Hub aggregates findings.

entries.name: Amazon Inspector
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Inspector is a vulnerability scanner for workloads.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Inspector scans supported EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and exposure.
entries.real_world_use_case: Find known CVEs in container images before deployment.
common_misconceptions: Inspector is not GuardDuty: vulnerabilities differ from suspicious activity.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Inspector scans vulnerabilities; GuardDuty detects threats; Systems Manager helps patch.

entries.name: AWS CloudTrail
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: CloudTrail is the audit trail showing who did what.
entries.plain_english_explanation: CloudTrail records AWS API calls and account activity for audit, governance, compliance, and security investigations.
entries.real_world_use_case: Investigate who changed a security group or deleted a bucket policy.
common_misconceptions: CloudTrail is not CloudWatch metrics/log monitoring.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: CloudTrail audits actions; Config tracks resource state; CloudWatch monitors telemetry.

entries.name: AWS Security Hub
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Security Hub is a central security findings scoreboard.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Security Hub aggregates and normalizes security findings from AWS services and partner tools and checks against security standards.
entries.real_world_use_case: Centralize GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config findings across accounts.
common_misconceptions: It does not replace the underlying scanners; it collects and prioritizes them.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Security Hub aggregates; GuardDuty detects; Inspector scans; Config evaluates.

entries.name: Amazon EC2
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: EC2 is renting virtual computers on demand.
entries.plain_english_explanation: EC2 provides resizable virtual servers called instances. You choose instance type, OS image, networking, storage, and scaling pattern, with more control and responsibility than serverless services.
entries.real_world_use_case: Run a custom web server or legacy application needing OS-level control.
common_misconceptions: EC2 is not automatically serverless; you manage OS/app/security choices.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: EC2 gives control; Lambda runs functions; ECS/EKS run containers; Beanstalk deploys apps.

entries.name: Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: An AMI is a stamped recipe for launching servers.
entries.plain_english_explanation: An AMI contains the operating system and software configuration needed to launch EC2 instances consistently.
entries.real_world_use_case: Create a hardened Linux image with monitoring agents preinstalled.
common_misconceptions: An AMI is not the running server; it is used to create one and is regional.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: AMI is server template; EBS snapshot is block-storage backup; instance type is hardware shape.

entries.name: EC2 instance families
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Instance families are vehicle classes for different jobs.
entries.plain_english_explanation: EC2 instance families are optimized for general purpose, compute, memory, storage, accelerated/GPU, and other workloads. Choosing the right family improves performance and cost.
entries.real_world_use_case: Use compute optimized for CPU-heavy jobs and memory optimized for in-memory databases.
common_misconceptions: Bigger is not always better; match workload bottleneck.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Instance family chooses shape; Auto Scaling changes quantity; Savings Plans/RIs affect price.

entries.name: Auto Scaling
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Auto Scaling is a thermostat for capacity.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Auto Scaling adjusts capacity to maintain availability and match demand. EC2 Auto Scaling groups launch/terminate instances using desired, min, max, and scaling policies.
entries.real_world_use_case: Add servers during traffic spikes and remove them overnight.
common_misconceptions: Auto Scaling is not a load balancer; it changes capacity.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Auto Scaling changes number of resources; ELB distributes traffic; CloudWatch can trigger scaling.

entries.name: Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A load balancer is a receptionist sending visitors to healthy desks.
entries.plain_english_explanation: ELB distributes traffic across targets such as EC2 instances, containers, and IPs, improving availability and routing around unhealthy targets.
entries.real_world_use_case: Put a load balancer in front of web servers in multiple AZs.
common_misconceptions: A load balancer does not create more servers; pair it with Auto Scaling.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: ALB routes HTTP; NLB handles high-performance TCP/UDP; CloudFront delivers at edge.

entries.name: Application Load Balancer (ALB)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: ALB is a smart web receptionist that reads URL paths and host names.
entries.plain_english_explanation: ALB handles HTTP/HTTPS layer-7 routing, including host/path rules and target groups, often for web apps and microservices.
entries.real_world_use_case: Route /api to API containers and /images to another target group.
common_misconceptions: ALB is not the best answer for raw TCP/UDP performance; use NLB.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: ALB = application layer HTTP; NLB = network layer TCP/UDP.

entries.name: Network Load Balancer (NLB)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: NLB directs traffic at road-intersection level without reading web pages.
entries.plain_english_explanation: NLB distributes TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic at high performance and low latency, with static IP and source-IP preservation patterns.
entries.real_world_use_case: Expose a high-throughput TCP service.
common_misconceptions: NLB does not do rich HTTP path routing like ALB.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: NLB = transport layer; ALB = HTTP app layer; CloudFront = CDN edge.

entries.name: AWS Lambda
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Lambda hires a worker only when a task arrives.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Lambda runs code without provisioning servers. It is event-driven and billed by requests/execution time while AWS manages the underlying servers.
entries.real_world_use_case: Process an uploaded S3 image or serve an API Gateway request.
common_misconceptions: Serverless still requires owning code, IAM, configuration, and cost controls.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Lambda runs functions; ECS/EKS run containers; EC2 runs servers.

entries.name: Amazon ECS and AWS Fargate
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: ECS schedules containers; Fargate lets AWS manage the container servers.
entries.plain_english_explanation: ECS runs containerized applications as tasks/services. Fargate is serverless compute for containers so you avoid managing EC2 worker nodes.
entries.real_world_use_case: Run a containerized API without Kubernetes or server administration.
common_misconceptions: Fargate is a compute option, not a separate orchestrator.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: ECS is AWS-native containers; EKS is Kubernetes; Fargate removes server management.

entries.name: Amazon EKS
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: EKS is AWS managing the Kubernetes control plane.
entries.plain_english_explanation: EKS runs Kubernetes on AWS for teams needing Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem while AWS manages control plane availability.
entries.real_world_use_case: Run portable Kubernetes microservices on AWS.
common_misconceptions: EKS is usually more complex than ECS for beginners.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: EKS = managed Kubernetes; ECS = AWS-native orchestrator; Fargate = serverless compute option.

entries.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Beanstalk plants the infrastructure around uploaded app code.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Elastic Beanstalk deploys and manages web apps using underlying AWS resources like EC2, Auto Scaling, and load balancers while preserving access to those resources.
entries.real_world_use_case: Deploy a simple Java, Node.js, Python, or .NET web app quickly.
common_misconceptions: Beanstalk is not the same as Lambda serverless functions; it often creates EC2 resources.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Beanstalk abstracts app deployment; CloudFormation provisions infrastructure; Lambda runs functions.

entries.name: Amazon S3
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: S3 is an almost limitless object-storage warehouse.
entries.plain_english_explanation: S3 stores objects in buckets and is highly durable. It is used for backups, static sites, logs, data lakes, media, and application assets.
entries.real_world_use_case: Store website images, analytics files, backups, and logs.
common_misconceptions: S3 is not a block disk for EC2 boot volumes; use EBS.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: S3 = object storage; EBS = block volume; EFS = shared file system.

entries.name: S3 storage classes
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Storage classes are shelf types for hot, cool, or archived boxes.
entries.plain_english_explanation: S3 storage classes trade access frequency, retrieval time, availability/resilience model, and cost. Standard is for active data; IA and Glacier classes reduce cost for colder data.
entries.real_world_use_case: Move old logs to cheaper archival classes.
common_misconceptions: The cheapest class can cost more if retrieved often or needed instantly.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Lifecycle moves objects; Intelligent-Tiering changes tiers by access; Glacier classes archive.

entries.name: S3 lifecycle policies
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Lifecycle is an automatic filing clerk moving or expiring objects by rule.
entries.plain_english_explanation: S3 lifecycle configuration transitions objects between classes or expires them based on age/prefix/tags for cost and retention management.
entries.real_world_use_case: Move logs after 30 days and delete after 7 years.
common_misconceptions: Lifecycle follows configured rules; it does not infer business value magically.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Lifecycle applies rules; Intelligent-Tiering monitors access; Backup coordinates backups.

entries.name: Amazon EBS
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: EBS is a virtual hard drive attached to an EC2 computer.
entries.plain_english_explanation: EBS provides block storage volumes for EC2, suitable for operating systems, databases, and low-latency disk needs.
entries.real_world_use_case: Attach a gp3 volume to an EC2 database server.
common_misconceptions: EBS is AZ-scoped and not shared global object storage.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: EBS = EC2 disk; EFS = shared file system; S3 = object store.

entries.name: Amazon EFS
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: EFS is a shared network folder for multiple Linux servers.
entries.plain_english_explanation: EFS is a scalable managed NFS file system that multiple EC2 instances can mount concurrently across AZs.
entries.real_world_use_case: Share uploaded user files across web servers.
common_misconceptions: EFS is not a Windows file server; FSx handles Windows file shares.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: EFS = Linux NFS; FSx = specialized file systems; EBS = single-instance block.

entries.name: Amazon FSx
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: FSx is AWS running specialized file servers for you.
entries.plain_english_explanation: FSx provides managed file systems including Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, and OpenZFS for protocol/performance-specific workloads.
entries.real_world_use_case: Migrate Windows shared drives or run HPC with Lustre.
common_misconceptions: FSx is not always the simplest shared-storage answer; EFS is simpler for Linux NFS.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: FSx = specialized managed file systems; EFS = elastic Linux NFS; S3 = object storage.

entries.name: S3 Glacier storage classes
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Glacier is a deep vault: cheap to keep, slower to retrieve.
entries.plain_english_explanation: S3 Glacier storage classes are for long-term archive data that is rarely accessed; retrieval time and fees depend on class and option.
entries.real_world_use_case: Archive compliance records or long-term backups.
common_misconceptions: Glacier is poor for frequently accessed application files.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: S3 Standard for active data; IA for less frequent; Glacier for archive.

entries.name: AWS Storage Gateway
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Storage Gateway translates on-premises storage habits to AWS storage.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Storage Gateway connects on-premises environments to cloud storage through file, volume, or tape gateway patterns for hybrid storage.
entries.real_world_use_case: Replace physical tapes with virtual tapes stored in AWS.
common_misconceptions: It is not a general VPN; it bridges storage use cases.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Storage Gateway connects storage; Direct Connect/VPN connect networks; DataSync moves data.

entries.name: AWS Backup
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: AWS Backup is a central scheduler and policy book for backups.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Backup centrally manages backup plans, retention, and recovery points across supported AWS services.
entries.real_world_use_case: Apply daily backups to EBS, RDS, and EFS resources.
common_misconceptions: It orchestrates backups; it does not replace understanding restore behavior per service.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Backup manages policies; EBS snapshots are one mechanism; S3 versioning/lifecycle protect objects.

entries.name: Amazon VPC
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A VPC is your private AWS neighborhood with streets, gates, and addresses.
entries.plain_english_explanation: VPC lets you define an isolated virtual network with IP ranges, subnets, route tables, gateways, and security controls.
entries.real_world_use_case: Put web servers in public subnets and databases in private subnets.
common_misconceptions: A VPC is regional and does not automatically make resources public/private.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: VPC is container; subnet is slice; route table controls paths; SG/NACL filter.

entries.name: Subnets
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A subnet is a street/block inside the VPC neighborhood.
entries.plain_english_explanation: A subnet is an IP range in one AZ. Public/private behavior comes from routing, especially whether there is a route to an internet gateway.
entries.real_world_use_case: Place load balancers in public subnets and app servers in private subnets.
common_misconceptions: Public/private is about routes, not just the name.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Subnet segments IPs; route table controls destination; NACL filters at subnet boundary.

entries.name: Route tables
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Route tables are road signs for network packets.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Route tables contain rules that direct traffic from subnets/gateways to local VPC, internet gateway, NAT gateway, transit gateway, VPN, and other targets.
entries.real_world_use_case: Route public subnet internet traffic to IGW and private subnet outbound traffic to NAT.
common_misconceptions: Security groups do not route traffic; they filter allowed traffic.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Route tables choose paths; SG/NACL filter; gateways connect networks.

entries.name: Internet Gateway (IGW)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: An IGW is the front gate connecting a VPC to the public internet.
entries.plain_english_explanation: An internet gateway enables communication between public VPC resources and the internet when routes, public addressing, and security rules allow it.
entries.real_world_use_case: Allow a public Application Load Balancer to receive internet traffic.
common_misconceptions: Attaching an IGW alone does not expose every resource.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: IGW enables direct internet path; NAT Gateway enables outbound-only path from private subnets.

entries.name: NAT Gateway
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: A NAT gateway is an outbound-only lobby for private servers.
entries.plain_english_explanation: NAT Gateway lets resources in private subnets initiate outbound IPv4 internet connections while preventing unsolicited inbound internet connections.
entries.real_world_use_case: Private EC2 instances download patches without public inbound access.
common_misconceptions: NAT is not a firewall and does not make private resources public.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: NAT Gateway = outbound from private; IGW = direct internet; VPC endpoint = private AWS service access.

entries.name: Security groups vs NACLs
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Security groups are room door locks; NACLs are street checkpoints.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Security groups are stateful resource-level firewalls; network ACLs are stateless subnet-level ordered allow/deny rules.
entries.real_world_use_case: Allow HTTPS to web instances with SGs and use NACLs as broad guardrails.
common_misconceptions: NACLs require inbound and outbound rules because they are stateless; SGs allow return traffic.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: SG = resource-level stateful allow rules; NACL = subnet-level stateless allow/deny.

entries.name: Amazon Route 53
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Route 53 is AWS DNS: the internet phonebook plus routing rules.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Route 53 maps domain names to targets and supports routing policies, health checks, and domain registration.
entries.real_world_use_case: Point example.com to CloudFront or fail over between endpoints.
common_misconceptions: Route 53 does not serve content; it tells clients where to go.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Route 53 = DNS/routing; CloudFront = CDN; ELB = traffic distribution to targets.

entries.name: Amazon CloudFront
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: CloudFront is a global cache that puts content near users.
entries.plain_english_explanation: CloudFront is a CDN that caches and delivers content through edge locations and integrates with S3, ALB, API Gateway, and WAF.
entries.real_world_use_case: Serve static assets globally with lower latency.
common_misconceptions: CloudFront is not the origin storage itself; it fetches from origins.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: CloudFront delivers/caches; S3 stores objects; Route 53 resolves names.

entries.name: AWS Direct Connect
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Direct Connect is a private leased road from your data center to AWS.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Direct Connect provides dedicated network connectivity from on-premises locations to AWS with more consistent performance than internet paths.
entries.real_world_use_case: Connect a data center to AWS for steady hybrid workloads.
common_misconceptions: Direct Connect is not encrypted by default like VPN; add encryption if required.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Direct Connect = dedicated connection; Site-to-Site VPN = encrypted tunnel over internet.

entries.name: AWS VPN
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: VPN is an encrypted tunnel through the public internet.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS VPN includes Site-to-Site VPN for network-to-VPC connections and Client VPN for user remote access.
entries.real_world_use_case: Connect an office network to a VPC quickly.
common_misconceptions: VPN performance depends on internet path; Direct Connect may be more predictable.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: VPN = encrypted internet tunnel; Direct Connect = dedicated link; Transit Gateway = hub.

entries.name: AWS Transit Gateway
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Transit Gateway is a central bus station for many VPCs and networks.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on-premises networks with a hub-and-spoke model, simplifying large topologies.
entries.real_world_use_case: Connect dozens of VPCs and hybrid links through one hub.
common_misconceptions: Detailed route-domain design is beyond CLF, but high-level purpose matters.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Transit Gateway connects many networks; peering is pairwise; Direct Connect/VPN connect on-premises.

entries.name: Amazon RDS
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: RDS is AWS doing database server chores for familiar relational databases.
entries.plain_english_explanation: RDS is a managed relational database service for engines such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2. AWS handles provisioning, backup, patching options, and availability features.
entries.real_world_use_case: Run a transactional e-commerce database without self-managing database servers.
common_misconceptions: AWS manages infrastructure chores but not your schema, data model, or query quality.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: RDS = managed relational engines; Aurora = AWS-optimized relational; DynamoDB = NoSQL.

entries.name: Amazon Aurora
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Aurora is an AWS-built high-performance relational engine compatible with MySQL/PostgreSQL.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Aurora is a managed cloud-optimized relational database with distributed storage and MySQL/PostgreSQL compatibility editions.
entries.real_world_use_case: Modernize a MySQL/PostgreSQL workload needing higher availability/performance.
common_misconceptions: Aurora is related to RDS experience but not identical to standard community MySQL on RDS.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Aurora = AWS-optimized relational; RDS = managed common engines; DynamoDB = NoSQL.

entries.name: Amazon DynamoDB
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: DynamoDB is a managed key-value/document table built for huge scale.
entries.plain_english_explanation: DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database with fast performance at scale for key-based access patterns.
entries.real_world_use_case: Store sessions, shopping carts, IoT state, or leaderboards.
common_misconceptions: It is not a drop-in replacement for relational joins and ad hoc SQL.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: DynamoDB = NoSQL; RDS/Aurora = relational SQL; ElastiCache = in-memory cache.

entries.name: Amazon ElastiCache
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: ElastiCache is a high-speed memory shelf for data needed again soon.
entries.plain_english_explanation: ElastiCache is managed in-memory caching compatible with Redis/Valkey and Memcached patterns, reducing latency and database load.
entries.real_world_use_case: Cache product catalog reads or session data.
common_misconceptions: A cache is usually not the durable system of record.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: ElastiCache = cache; RDS/DynamoDB = databases; MemoryDB = durable Redis-compatible database.

entries.name: Amazon Redshift
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Redshift is a data warehouse for scanning lots of structured records.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Redshift is a managed analytics warehouse optimized for complex queries over large datasets, not small transaction updates.
entries.real_world_use_case: Analyze years of sales data for business dashboards.
common_misconceptions: Not ideal for high-frequency transaction processing.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Redshift = warehouse; Athena = query S3; RDS = transactional relational DB.

entries.name: Amazon Athena
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Athena lets you ask SQL questions directly against files in S3.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Athena is a serverless interactive query service for analyzing S3 data with SQL. You pay per query/data scanned and manage no servers.
entries.real_world_use_case: Query application logs stored in S3.
common_misconceptions: Athena does not store data; S3 stores it.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Athena queries S3; Redshift is a warehouse; Glue catalogs/transforms data.

entries.name: AWS Glue
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Glue is a data prep workshop plus catalog.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Glue is serverless data integration for ETL, data cataloging, and preparing analytics data. Glue Data Catalog metadata is used by Athena and others.
entries.real_world_use_case: Catalog S3 data and transform CSV logs to Parquet.
common_misconceptions: Glue is not the dashboarding tool.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Glue catalogs/transforms; Athena queries; QuickSight visualizes.

entries.name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: OpenSearch is a fast searchable index for logs and text.
entries.plain_english_explanation: OpenSearch Service manages OpenSearch for search, log analytics, and observability-style indexing/querying.
entries.real_world_use_case: Search application logs or power website search.
common_misconceptions: Not a relational transaction database replacement.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: OpenSearch = search/log index; CloudWatch Logs = log collection; Athena = SQL over S3.

entries.name: Amazon QuickSight
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: QuickSight is a dashboard and BI studio.
entries.plain_english_explanation: QuickSight creates dashboards, visualizations, and embedded analytics from sources such as Athena, Redshift, RDS, and S3.
entries.real_world_use_case: Build executive cost or sales dashboards.
common_misconceptions: It does not store/prepare all source data by itself.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: QuickSight visualizes; Redshift/Athena query; Glue prepares/catalogs.

entries.name: Amazon SQS
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: SQS is a waiting line for work messages.
entries.plain_english_explanation: SQS is a managed message queue that decouples components and buffers work when producers and consumers run at different speeds.
entries.real_world_use_case: Queue order-processing jobs during traffic spikes.
common_misconceptions: SQS is not pub/sub fanout by itself; SNS commonly handles fanout.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: SQS = queue; SNS = topic broadcast; EventBridge = event router.

entries.name: Amazon SNS
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: SNS is a megaphone broadcasting to subscribers.
entries.plain_english_explanation: SNS is a managed pub/sub service where publishers send to topics and subscribers such as email, SMS, HTTP, Lambda, or SQS receive messages.
entries.real_world_use_case: Send one order event to email alerts, Lambda, and a queue.
common_misconceptions: SNS is not primarily a work queue for one worker group; use SQS.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: SNS broadcasts; SQS queues; EventBridge routes structured events.

entries.name: Amazon EventBridge
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: EventBridge is an event router with rules.
entries.plain_english_explanation: EventBridge is a serverless event bus connecting AWS services, SaaS partners, and custom applications using event patterns and targets.
entries.real_world_use_case: Route order-created events to workflows and notification targets.
common_misconceptions: It is broader than a simple queue or notification topic.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: EventBridge routes events; SNS broadcasts; SQS buffers work; Step Functions orchestrates.

entries.name: AWS Step Functions
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Step Functions is a flowchart runner for workflows.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Step Functions coordinates multi-step workflows with state machines, retries, branching, parallelism, and visual execution history.
entries.real_world_use_case: Coordinate order validation, payment, inventory, and notification.
common_misconceptions: It coordinates compute but is not the compute itself.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Step Functions orchestrates; Lambda/ECS perform tasks; EventBridge routes events.

entries.name: Amazon API Gateway
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs.
entries.plain_english_explanation: API Gateway creates, publishes, secures, monitors, and manages APIs, often in front of Lambda or HTTP backends.
entries.real_world_use_case: Expose a serverless REST API backed by Lambda.
common_misconceptions: Business logic usually lives behind it, not inside it.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: API Gateway fronts APIs; ALB balances web traffic; CloudFront caches at edge.

entries.name: Amazon CloudWatch
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: CloudWatch is the dashboard, alarm system, and log notebook.
entries.plain_english_explanation: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, events, and alarms for AWS resources and applications to monitor health and trigger actions.
entries.real_world_use_case: Alarm on high EC2 CPU and inspect Lambda logs.
common_misconceptions: CloudWatch is not the audit record of API calls; CloudTrail is.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: CloudWatch monitors telemetry; CloudTrail audits API calls; Config tracks configuration.

entries.name: AWS CloudFormation
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: CloudFormation is a blueprint that builds resources repeatably.
entries.plain_english_explanation: CloudFormation provisions infrastructure as code using templates and stacks, enabling repeatable create/update/delete operations.
entries.real_world_use_case: Deploy a VPC, subnets, security groups, and EC2 from a template.
common_misconceptions: It is not just an app deployer; it is general IaC.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: CloudFormation defines infrastructure; Beanstalk deploys apps; CDK synthesizes CloudFormation.

entries.name: AWS Systems Manager
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Systems Manager is a remote operations toolbox.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Systems Manager helps view/control resources, run commands, patch servers, automate operations, and store parameters.
entries.real_world_use_case: Patch EC2 fleets or run a command across instances.
common_misconceptions: It is a suite of capabilities, not one single dashboard.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Systems Manager operates resources; CloudWatch monitors; Config evaluates state.

entries.name: AWS Config
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Config is a configuration recorder and rule checker.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Config records resource configuration changes and evaluates them against compliance rules.
entries.real_world_use_case: Detect public S3 buckets or risky security groups.
common_misconceptions: Config is not CloudTrail; it focuses on resource state, not every API event.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Config tracks state/compliance; CloudTrail audits actions; Security Hub aggregates findings.

entries.name: AWS Organizations
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Organizations is a company org chart for multiple AWS accounts.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Organizations centrally manages multiple AWS accounts with consolidated billing, OUs, and service control policies.
entries.real_world_use_case: Separate dev, test, prod, and security accounts under one payer.
common_misconceptions: SCPs set maximum permissions but do not grant access by themselves.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Organizations manages accounts/billing/guardrails; IAM grants within accounts; Control Tower sets baselines.

entries.name: AWS Control Tower
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Control Tower is a governed multi-account landing-zone setup.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Control Tower sets up and governs AWS multi-account environments using best-practice blueprints, guardrails, and account factory.
entries.real_world_use_case: Launch new accounts with baseline logging and security controls.
common_misconceptions: It uses Organizations underneath and does not replace account/OUs/SCP understanding.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Control Tower creates governed baseline; Organizations manages accounts; Config/Security Hub monitor.

entries.name: AWS Trusted Advisor
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Trusted Advisor is a checklist consultant scanning for improvement opportunities.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations for cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service quotas, and operational excellence, with check access varying by support plan.
entries.real_world_use_case: Find idle resources, exposed ports, or quota warnings.
common_misconceptions: It recommends; it does not automatically fix everything. Full checks vary by support plan.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Trusted Advisor recommends; Cost Explorer analyzes spend; Security Hub aggregates security findings.

entries.name: AWS Health Dashboard
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Health Dashboard shows AWS events that may affect you.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Health provides service event visibility and account/resource-specific notifications for planned changes or incidents.
entries.real_world_use_case: See whether a service issue affects resources in your account.
common_misconceptions: Public status is broad; AWS Health can be personalized.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Health shows AWS/service events; CloudWatch shows workload metrics; CloudTrail shows actions.

entries.name: AWS pricing models
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Pricing is choosing pay-as-you-go rides, committed passes, or spare-seat discounts.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS pricing includes On-Demand flexibility, Reserved Instances/Savings Plans commitments, Spot spare capacity, Free Tier, and volume/usage-based pricing patterns.
entries.real_world_use_case: Use On-Demand for experiments, Savings Plans for steady compute, Spot for batch jobs.
common_misconceptions: The biggest discount is not always best; commitments require predictable usage and Spot can interrupt.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Pricing model decides how you pay; Cost Explorer analyzes spend; Budgets alerts.

entries.name: AWS Savings Plans
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Savings Plans are a commitment coupon for steady dollars-per-hour usage.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Savings Plans provide lower prices in exchange for a one- or three-year usage commitment, especially for compute usage.
entries.real_world_use_case: Commit to baseline production compute spend.
common_misconceptions: Savings Plans do not reserve capacity by themselves.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Savings Plans = flexible compute discount; RIs = reservation/discount model; On-Demand = no commitment.

entries.name: Reserved Instances
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Reserved Instances are booking a server class in advance for a discount.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Reserved Instances discount eligible instance usage in exchange for term commitment, and some options can provide capacity reservation benefits.
entries.real_world_use_case: Reduce cost for a database server that runs continuously.
common_misconceptions: RIs are less flexible than many Savings Plans and poor for unpredictable workloads.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: RIs = specific reservations/discounts; Savings Plans = flexible spend commitments; Spot = interruptible spare capacity.

entries.name: AWS Cost Explorer
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Cost Explorer is a spending graph and filter tool.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Cost Explorer visualizes, filters, and analyzes AWS costs and usage over time to find trends and cost drivers.
entries.real_world_use_case: Find which service or account caused a bill increase.
common_misconceptions: It is not primarily an alerting tool; Budgets alerts.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Cost Explorer analyzes; Budgets alerts; CUR provides raw detailed data.

entries.name: AWS Budgets
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Budgets is a spending smoke alarm.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Budgets sets custom cost, usage, reservation, and Savings Plans thresholds and sends alerts on actual or forecasted values.
entries.real_world_use_case: Alert when dev account spend is forecast to exceed $500.
common_misconceptions: Budgets alerts; it does not automatically prevent every spend unless paired with controls/actions.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Budgets alerts; Cost Explorer investigates; Organizations/SCPs enforce guardrails.

entries.name: AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: CUR is the detailed itemized AWS receipt.
entries.plain_english_explanation: CUR provides detailed billing and usage line items, commonly delivered to S3 for analysis with Athena, Redshift, or QuickSight.
entries.real_world_use_case: Build chargeback/showback by account, tag, service, and usage type.
common_misconceptions: CUR is raw and more detailed than Cost Explorer; it requires analysis tooling.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: CUR = raw detailed data; Cost Explorer = interactive UI; Budgets = alerts.

entries.name: Consolidated billing
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Consolidated billing is one family bill for many AWS accounts.
entries.plain_english_explanation: With AWS Organizations, consolidated billing combines charges from member accounts under one management/payer account and may share eligible volume discounts.
entries.real_world_use_case: Pay for dev, prod, and security accounts through one organization.
common_misconceptions: It does not merge security boundaries; accounts remain separate.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Consolidated billing aggregates payment; SCPs set guardrails; Cost Explorer analyzes linked-account spend.

entries.name: AWS Support plans
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Support plans are service-desk tiers with different response times and guidance.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Support plans range from Basic to Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, and Enterprise, with increasing support response levels and entitlements.
entries.real_world_use_case: Choose Business Support for production workloads needing 24/7 technical support access.
common_misconceptions: Basic includes account/billing support and docs, not the same technical support response levels.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Support plan = support entitlement; Trusted Advisor = recommendations; Health = service events.

entries.name: AWS Marketplace
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Marketplace is an app store for third-party software billed through AWS.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Marketplace is a catalog for finding, buying, deploying, and managing third-party software, data, and services, often integrated with AWS billing.
entries.real_world_use_case: Subscribe to a security appliance AMI or SaaS monitoring tool.
common_misconceptions: Marketplace products are not all AWS-built services; review vendor/pricing/licensing.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Marketplace = third-party offerings; Service Catalog = approved internal catalogs; AWS services = native services.

entries.name: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: DMS is a moving truck for databases with ongoing replication.
entries.plain_english_explanation: DMS helps migrate databases to AWS or between databases with minimal downtime for supported sources and targets; heterogeneous migrations may need schema conversion.
entries.real_world_use_case: Move on-premises MySQL or Oracle to RDS/Aurora.
common_misconceptions: DMS moves data; schema conversion can require SCT for different engines.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: DMS migrates databases; Application Migration Service migrates servers; Snowball moves bulk offline data.

entries.name: AWS Snowball / Snow Family
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Snowball is a rugged shipping container for data.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Snow Family devices move large data sets into/out of AWS and support edge/disconnected compute where network transfer is impractical.
entries.real_world_use_case: Transfer hundreds of terabytes to S3 without saturating internet links.
common_misconceptions: Not for small routine transfers where normal upload is practical.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Snowball = physical transfer; DataSync = online movement; Storage Gateway = hybrid storage.

entries.name: AWS Migration Hub
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Migration Hub is the project dashboard for migrations.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Migration Hub provides central visibility into application migration progress across AWS and partner migration tools.
entries.real_world_use_case: Track migration waves for dozens of applications.
common_misconceptions: It tracks and organizes; it is not the data mover for every workload.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Migration Hub tracks; DMS migrates databases; Application Migration Service rehosts servers.

entries.name: AWS Application Migration Service
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Application Migration Service is a lift-and-shift copier for servers.
entries.plain_english_explanation: AWS Application Migration Service continuously replicates source servers and launches them as EC2 instances for rehost migrations.
entries.real_world_use_case: Lift and shift on-premises application servers to EC2.
common_misconceptions: It is not database-specific; DMS handles database migrations.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Application Migration Service migrates servers; DMS migrates databases; Migration Hub tracks.

entries.name: Amazon Bedrock
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Bedrock is a managed doorway to foundation models.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Bedrock is a fully managed service for building generative AI applications with foundation models from AWS and third-party providers.
entries.real_world_use_case: Build a chatbot or content generation workflow without managing model servers.
common_misconceptions: Bedrock is not the broad platform for training every custom ML model; SageMaker is broader for ML lifecycle.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Bedrock = foundation models/genAI apps; SageMaker = ML build/train/deploy; AI services = prebuilt APIs.

entries.name: Amazon SageMaker
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: SageMaker is a workshop for building, training, and deploying ML models.
entries.plain_english_explanation: SageMaker is a managed ML platform for data prep, training, tuning, deployment, and MLOps. CLF learners mainly need high-level recognition.
entries.real_world_use_case: Train and deploy a custom fraud detection model.
common_misconceptions: CLF-C02 does not require hands-on model engineering depth.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: SageMaker builds custom ML; Bedrock uses foundation models; Rekognition/Textract/Comprehend are prebuilt APIs.

entries.name: Amazon Comprehend
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Comprehend is a text-understanding API.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Comprehend uses NLP to find sentiment, key phrases, entities, topics, and language in text.
entries.real_world_use_case: Analyze customer reviews for sentiment and common issues.
common_misconceptions: It is not a general database search engine.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Comprehend = text NLP; Textract = document text/forms; Transcribe = speech to text.

entries.name: Amazon Rekognition
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Rekognition is a computer-vision API for images and video.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Rekognition analyzes images/video for labels, objects, faces, text, moderation categories, and visual information.
entries.real_world_use_case: Detect unsafe image uploads or tag media libraries.
common_misconceptions: It does not store your whole media catalog by itself.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Rekognition = image/video; Textract = document extraction; Comprehend = text meaning.

entries.name: Amazon Transcribe
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Transcribe turns speech into written text.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Transcribe is automatic speech recognition for converting audio into text for calls, subtitles, and search.
entries.real_world_use_case: Create searchable transcripts of support calls.
common_misconceptions: It is not text-to-speech; Polly does that.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Transcribe = speech to text; Polly = text to speech; Comprehend = understand text.

entries.name: Amazon Textract
entries.teaching_goal: Build a practical mental model first, then connect it to CLF-C02 clue language.
entries.simple_analogy: Textract reads documents and forms, not just plain OCR text.
entries.plain_english_explanation: Textract extracts text, handwriting, forms, and tables from scanned documents and images for document automation.
entries.real_world_use_case: Extract fields from invoices or scanned applications.
common_misconceptions: It is not general image recognition; it focuses on document structure.
entries.adjacent_services_comparison: Textract = document extraction; Rekognition = image/video; Comprehend = NLP.
